transcript.text: Hi! Could you pull which customers spent less this quarter than last quarter? I'm thinking of sending them something to bring them back, maybe a 15% coupon. The sales export is attached. [shares sales.csv]

Thanks, that's clear. You want the customers whose spending dropped from last quarter to this one, so you can decide who gets a win-back offer like a 15% coupon. I've looked at the export. It has 2,020 orders from about 1,002 customers, and the latest order is 29 March 2026. So I'd compare this quarter (January to March) with the quarter before it, and count only paid orders, not refunded or cancelled ones. Tell me if either of those is wrong. Before I pull the list, who do you want on it? One option is everyone whose spend dipped by any amount. The other is only the customers who have really drifted away, meaning a big drop or no orders at all this quarter. Someone who spent only a little less probably doesn't need a coupon, while a customer who has vanished probably does.

Paid-only sounds right, but I'm not sure what labels the status column uses, so please check that refunded and cancelled orders are really excluded before we compare quarters. Also, I can only send 1,000 coupons, and my real aim is to reach customers who are slipping away but would still respond, not everyone whose spend dipped a little. So I need the list ranked, not just filtered. Ideally I'd also avoid customers who look like they'd buy anyway, though I'm not sure how to tell that from this data. The campaign goes out on the 15th, and the marketing manager has to approve the list first, so I need something I can explain. I'm strong in Excel and pivot tables but haven't built a model before, so please keep the method simple enough for me to check in a pivot. How would you rank them, and where would the cutoff for 1,000 fall?

The status column uses exactly three labels: paid (1,733 orders), refunded (188) and cancelled (99). Counting paid orders only drops the other two cleanly. I'll keep "this quarter" as January to March and "last quarter" as October to December, unless you tell me otherwise. **Your 1,000 limit probably won't bind.**
- Only 324 customers had a paid order last quarter, so at most 324 can have spent less than they did then. - Only 938 customers in the whole file have ever had a paid order. - So the cutoff has to come from a business rule, such as "stop where the drop is too small to justify 15% off". It can't come from the cap. - A ranked list still helps, because it shows where to stop. **How I'd rank them.** I'd use the dollar drop from last quarter to this one, with customers who have no paid order this quarter flagged. I'd also show the days since each customer's last paid order. Every column would be a pivot you could rebuild. **Telling who would buy anyway.** The table can't do this properly. It has no record of past coupons, so we can't see who responds to an offer. The best I can do is a proxy from purchase habits, such as customers whose spend held up or who ordered very recently. The only way to learn who really responds is to hold back a random group in this campaign. Here are three ways to go. Which fits best?

choices.title: Ranked win-back list you can rebuild in a pivot
choices.what: From paid orders only, I compute each customer's spend last quarter and this quarter, the dollar and percent drop, and the days since their last paid order. I rank by dollar drop, flag customers with no paid order this quarter, and mark those who look like they'd buy anyway (spend held up, or a very recent order). You get a file plus a short note listing each rule so the marketing manager can follow it. You get: A ranked customer list with every column behind the rank, a count of how many fall under each definition of 'slipping' (any drop, big drop, none at all), and where a sensible cutoff would fall. Trade-off: It ranks by how far spend has fallen, not by who will respond to a coupon. This table has no record of past offers, so response can't be measured, only guessed from purchase habits. Effort: Quick: the list can be ready well before the 15th.

choices.title: Campaign plan with a built-in test of who responds
choices.what: A written brief for you and the marketing manager. It sets out who to include and why, how to use the coupon budget, and how to hold back a random group of eligible customers so that after the campaign you can see who really came back because of the coupon and who would have bought anyway. You get: A decision-ready recommendation: eligibility rules, a cutoff you can defend, a holdout design and what to measure afterwards. Trade-off: It answers 'who responds' only after the campaign has run, and a holdout means a few eligible customers won't get a coupon this time. Effort: Moderate: a short brief, built on the same ranked numbers.

choices.title: A model that scores each customer's chance of stopping
choices.what: DCLab builds a prediction model on earlier quarters to estimate which customers are likely to stop buying next quarter, tested on data it hasn't seen, and scores every current customer. You get: A probability of lapsing for each customer and an honest measure of how well it works. Trade-off: Harder to explain and impossible to check in a pivot. It predicts who will lapse, not who the coupon will win back, so it doesn't settle the 'would buy anyway' question either. Effort: Longer: needs a definition of 'lapsed' and a check for columns that leak the answer.

transcript.text: are my business customers different from the normal ones?

I understand you want to know whether your business customers behave differently from your regular ones. What made you ask? Is there a decision behind it, like pricing, how you serve them, or where to put your effort?
We're thinking about hiring someone to look after the company members. Not sure yet. I just want to know if they're different from the freelancers.

Thanks, that helps. You're weighing whether a dedicated person for company members would be worth it, and you want to see if they really are a different kind of customer from the freelancers. Do you have a table or export of your members that shows which ones are companies and which are freelancers? If so, what does it say about each of them, for example what they pay, how much they use the service, or how long they stay? Please share it if you can.

It's a spreadsheet from our booking software, with member type, start date, plan, monthly fee, months as a member and complaints. I haven't really gone through it. What's the easiest way to show it to you?

The easiest way is to attach the file here in the chat, as it came out of the booking software. CSV or Excel is fine. You don't need to tidy it first, because I'll look through it with you. Those columns are what we need to compare company members and freelancers on fee, time as a member and complaints. Once it's in, I'll check how many of each type you have. One question while you attach it: will you be the one deciding on the hire, or does someone else need to see the answer too?
I'm the one deciding, yes. Need to know by end of November. I'll try to export it from the booking software and send it over. Not sure how to get it out of there yet though.

Thanks, that's clear: you decide, and you need the answer by the end of November, so there's time, but let's not leave the export too long. Most booking tools have an "Export" or "Download" button on the members or customers list, or under Reports, and it usually gives a CSV or Excel file. Which booking software do you use? Then I can point you to where that button is likely to be.
Not sure what it's called. It's the system we use for desk bookings and member sign-ups. Can't you just tell me how to find the export from there?

I can't say exactly where the button is without knowing the software, but this is where to look:

- **Find the name.** It's usually on the login page, in the browser tab or web address, at the top of the screen, or on the invoice you pay for it. Whoever set it up for you will also know. - **Find the list.** Open the page that lists your members, which may be called Members, Customers, Contacts or Accounts. Look for a button marked **Export**, **Download**, **CSV** or **Excel**. It's often at the top right, behind a "⋯" or "More" menu, or under **Reports**. - **If there's no button,** search the software's help for "export members". As a last resort, you can select the list on screen, copy it, and paste it into a blank spreadsheet. If you get stuck, send me a screenshot of the members page and I'll tell you what to click. You described it as a spreadsheet from the booking software. Do you already have that file saved somewhere, or would you have to pull it fresh from the system?
I think I have a file from a while back, but I can't remember where I saved it. I'd probably have to pull it again. I don't really know the name of the software, sorry.

The software name doesn't matter, and an old file is fine for a first look. If it has member type, plan, monthly fee, months as a member and complaints, I can start with it. A fresh export can follow later. Here is where to look for the old file:
- **Downloads folder.** Sort it by date and look for a spreadsheet (.xlsx or .csv). - **Search your computer.** Search for ".xlsx" or ".csv", or for words like "members" or "export". - **Your email.** You may have sent it to yourself or a colleague, so search your sent mail for attachments. If it isn't in any of those places, who set up the booking system or pays for it? They would know its name and could pull the export for you in a couple of minutes.
Ok, I'll look in my downloads and email later. I'm not sure who set the system up though.

That's fine, you don't need to know who set it up. Someone who uses it day to day can pull the export just as well. The software's name is usually on the page where members sign up or book a desk, or on the invoice for the subscription. Is there anyone on your team who handles member sign-ups, desk bookings or the bills? If there is, they could do the export in a couple of minutes. Whenever you find the old file or get a fresh one, attach it here and I'll start by counting how many company members and freelancers you have.
Maybe. I think the office manager does the bills, but I'm not sure. I'll look in my downloads and ask around this week and send whatever I find.

That plan works. Look in your downloads and email, ask the office manager, and send whatever you find. A screenshot of the members page would also help if you get stuck. While you look, here are three ways I could help. I'm assuming two things, so tell me if either is wrong:
- Your file has one row per member, with a member type that separates companies from freelancers. - By "different" you mean what they pay, how long they stay and how often they complain. Which of these would you like me to do once the file arrives?

transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline number, and give the 3% base rate next to it. **Why PR-AUC**

transcript.text: how can I analyze my customer [shares customers.csv]

I looked at customers.csv. It has 1,200 customers, with their plan, segment, city, signup date, how long they've been with you, monthly spend, recent support tickets, and a column showing whether they left the next month. In a first look, customers on the basic plan seem to leave more often than those on the other plans. That's only a first impression, and there are many ways to go from here. What would you like to be able to do or decide once you've analyzed your customers? For example, you might want to keep more of them, find out who is worth the most, or something else.
I want to see my customer groups, so I can treat each group a little different. Not sure what the best way to split them is.

Thanks, that helps. You want to split your customers into groups so you can handle each one a bit differently, and you're not sure what the best split is. The best split depends on what you'd do with it. Say a group is picked out tomorrow: what would you change for them? For example, you might send a retention offer to people likely to leave, give your best spenders special service, or support newer customers differently. Which of those is closest, or is it something else?
Mostly the ones who might leave. We want to keep them. The big spenders matter too, I guess. I'm not really sure how to pick the groups though.
Who will use these groups day to day? Is it you, or a team such as support, sales or marketing?
Me, mostly. I'm the one looking at this. I might pass it on to my team later, but I'm not sure yet.

Thanks. Since you're the one using this, I'll keep it simple. Nothing in the table gives away who leaves, so either route is safe to try. You told me you want to keep the customers who might leave, and big spenders matter too. So the real choice is whether the groups come from similar behaviour or from the risk of leaving. Here are two ways to do it:

choices.title: Find natural customer groups
choices.what: DCLab looks for groups that already exist in your data, using how long people have been customers, what they spend, their plan and how many support tickets they raised. Then it shows how many customers are in each group, their average spend, and how many of them left. You get: A handful of named groups (for example big spenders, new low-spend customers) with a profile of each, and which ones leave most. Trade-off: Groups come from similar behaviour, not from a forecast, so they show who tends to leave but don't score each person. You can't tell in advance which individual will leave. Effort: Light: a first set of groups to look at and react to.

choices.title: Predict who might leave
choices.what: DCLab builds a model that gives each customer a likelihood of leaving next month, learned from your past customers using churned_next_month. It is tested on customers it hasn't seen. You then sort customers into risk bands (high, medium, low) and can cross them with monthly_spend to single out big spenders at risk. You get: A risk score per customer, a check of how well it works, and risk groups you can act on, such as a retention list. Trade-off: It centres on leaving, so it says less about other ways your customers differ. It needs a bit more care to check that it works. Effort: Moderate: a model to build, test and explain.

transcript.text: I guess the second one, the one about who might leave. That's the part we need most. Not sure what the other one would give us, to be honest.

Good, we'll build a model that predicts which customers might leave next month. I checked the table first, and no column gives away the answer. Nothing looks like it was recorded after the customer left, so the model can use all the columns in the table. - **What DCLab builds:** The model learns from customers who stayed and customers who left. It uses their plan, segment, city, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and signup date. It gives each customer a likelihood of leaving. The customer ID is only a label, so the model won't use it. - **How it's tested:** DCLab keeps part of your customers aside and checks the model on them. That shows how well it would work on customers it hasn't seen. - **What you get:** You get a score for each customer, and the test results. You also see which things matter most for leaving. You can sort customers into groups by risk, such as high, medium and low. You can then split those groups by monthly spend to see the big spenders who are at risk. That covers the two things you told me you care about. In a quick look at the table, basic plan customers leave most often and plus customers least, with premium in between. That is only a starting picture. The model will show whether plan really drives leaving, or whether something else does. You'll see the results once DCLab has run them. I won't guess at how accurate it will be until then.
